newsitem.title: USA: U.S. economy slows in third quarter, inflation mute.
newsitem.headline: U.S. economy slows in third quarter, inflation mute.

text.p: Consumers braked their spending and slowed the pace of economic expansion sharply in the third quarter, the Commerce Department said on Wednesday, helping to further drive inflation into the ground.

The nation's gross domestic product expanded at a 2.2 percent annual rate in the three months from July through September -- less than half the booming 4.7 percent pace posted during the second quarter.

Analysts said slower GDP growth, especially since it was accompanied by weaker price rises and mounting inventories of unsold goods, likely meant Federal Reserve policymakers would keep interest rates steady at their next meeting on Nov. 13.

"This is the next best thing to apple pie," said economist Anthony Chan of Banc One Investment Advisors Corp. in Columbus, Ohio. "It tells us that there's much less likelihood of super-accelerated growth in the fourth quarter."
GDP measures the value of all goods and services produced within a country's borders.

Consumer spending, which fuels two-thirds of national economic activity, barely grew between July and September, rising by 0.4 percent at a $5.2 billion annual rate after surging 3.4 percent at a $38.5 billion rate in the second quarter. It was the smallest gain in consumer spending in nearly five years, since it dropped 1 percent in the fourth quarter of 1991.
Partly as a result, stocks of unsold goods swelled at a $39.6 billion annual rate in the third quarter, more than five times the $7.1 billion rate of increase in the second quarter.
The department said inventories piled up at the fastest rate in 18 months, since they increased at a rate of $54.5 billion in the first quarter of last year.
Less than a week from next Tuesday's general elections, dueling politicians put their own opposing spin on the GDP figures.
Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole said slower growth was proof of "the myth of the Clinton recovery (that) has long been known to anxious wage-earners."
Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor countered that it showed the United States was in the midst of a balanced and sustained expansion that rolls on after six years of unbroken growth.

Robert Dederick, economic consultant to Northern Trust Co. in Chicago, said the fallback in growth to a pace generally considered sustainable without generating inflation likely helps the Clinton administration.
He added it would induce the Federal Reserve's policymakers to keep interest rates steady at their policy session two weeks from now.
"Essentially it says there's no need to twiddle with the dials for the time being at least," Dederick said.

The inflation-sensitive bond market initially rallied on the news, but a later report from the Commerce Department showing new-home sales fell by a smaller-than expected amount wiped out the bond market gains.

The Commerce Department reported that new home sales fell 0.5 percent in September to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 816,000. Wall Street analysts had expected sales to drop to a 768,000 annual rate in September.

The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was off 10/32 of a point, or $3.125 per $1,000 face value, at midday and its yield, which moves in the opposite direction, rose to 6.71 percent from 6.68 percent Tuesday.
Strong housing sales generally boost consumer spending as buyers furnish their new homes.

Analysts were uncertain whether spending would bounce back in the fourth quarter. Relatively strong levels of consumer confidence and steady income gains from an expanding job market are expected to bolster Christmas shopping.

But Chan of Banc One said he thought high levels of consumer debt would help further dampen fourth-quarter GDP growth to a 2 percent rate. Dederick said the inventory buildup would hold final quarter expansion to a range around 2.5 percent to 2.75 percent.
"Some of the buildup was clearly voluntary but some nearly certainly was involuntary and may come back to bite us on the production side," Dederick noted.
Inventory-building benefits the economy in the period during which it occurs, but it can become a drag if goods remain unsold because producers cut back to sell off stocks.
"The deceleration in (third-quarter) GDP growth was moderated by accelerations in inventory investment and in producers' durable equipment," the Commerce Department noted.
Federal government outlays dropped 4 percent at a $4.7 billion annual rate after growing 9.4 percent at a $10.5 billion rate in the second quarter.
Two price measures in the GDP report suggested virtually no inflation threat.

The implicit price deflator advanced at a 1.6 percent annual rate in the third quarter, compared with 1.8 percent in the second quarter, while the fixed-weights measure of price changes rose 1.9 percent, compared with 2.2 percent in the second quarter.
